edges.prereq: Dependency relationship, property 'condition' specifies hard or soft

nodes.name: Propositional Logic
nodes.description: The study of propositions combined with logical connectives such as and, or, not, and implication, with truth tables defining their meaning.

nodes.name: Direct Proofs
nodes.description: A proof technique establishing an implication by assuming the hypothesis and deducing the conclusion through a chain of valid logical steps.

nodes.name: Proof by Contraposition
nodes.description: Proving an implication 'p implies q' by instead proving its logically equivalent contrapositive, 'not q implies not p'.

nodes.name: Proof by Contradiction
nodes.description: Proving a statement by assuming its negation and deriving a logical contradiction, forcing the original statement to be true.

nodes.name: Simple Induction
nodes.description: Mathematical induction proving a statement for all naturals by establishing a base case and an inductive step from n to n+1.

nodes.name: Strong Induction
nodes.description: A variant of induction whose inductive step may assume the statement for all smaller values, not just the immediate predecessor.

nodes.name: Well-Ordering Principle
nodes.description: The principle that every nonempty set of natural numbers contains a least element, equivalent to and underpinning induction.

nodes.name: Structural Induction
nodes.description: Induction over recursively defined structures, proving a property holds for base cases and is preserved by the construction rules.

nodes.name: Stable Matching Problem
nodes.description: The problem of pairing two sides given preferences so that no two unmatched participants both prefer each other over their assigned partners.

nodes.name: Gale-Shapley Algorithm
nodes.description: The Gale-Shapley deferred-acceptance algorithm producing a stable matching through rounds of proposals and tentative acceptances.

nodes.name: Matching Optimality
nodes.description: The result that Gale-Shapley yields the matching most preferred by every member of the proposing side among all stable matchings.

nodes.name: Matching Pessimality
nodes.description: The corresponding result that the proposing-side-optimal matching is simultaneously the worst stable matching for the receiving side.

nodes.name: Graph Basics
nodes.description: Graphs as sets of vertices joined by edges, with the fundamental notions of degree, paths, connectivity, and cycles.

nodes.name: Eulerian Tours
nodes.description: Closed walks traversing every edge exactly once, existing precisely when a graph is connected with all vertices of even degree.

nodes.name: Trees
nodes.description: Connected acyclic graphs, equivalently graphs with a unique path between any two vertices, having exactly one fewer edge than vertices.

nodes.name: Planar Graphs
nodes.description: Graphs drawable in the plane without edge crossings, constrained by Euler's formula relating vertices, edges, and faces.

nodes.name: Hypercubes
nodes.description: Recursively defined hypercube graphs whose vertices are binary strings, with edges joining strings that differ in a single bit.

nodes.name: Euclid's Algorithm
nodes.description: Euclid's algorithm computing the greatest common divisor of two integers by repeatedly replacing the larger with its remainder modulo the smaller.

nodes.name: Extended Euclid
nodes.description: The extended Euclidean algorithm computing Bézout coefficients that express the gcd as an integer combination, yielding modular inverses.

nodes.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
nodes.description: The Chinese remainder theorem giving a unique solution modulo the product for a system of congruences with pairwise coprime moduli.

nodes.name: Fermat's Little Theorem
nodes.description: Fermat's little theorem stating that a raised to the power p minus one is congruent to one modulo a prime p not dividing a.

nodes.name: Symmetric Cryptography
nodes.description: Encryption schemes where sender and receiver share a single secret key used for both encryption and decryption of messages.

nodes.name: RSA Setup and Encryption
nodes.description: The RSA public-key scheme generating keys from two large primes and encrypting messages by modular exponentiation with the public exponent.

nodes.name: RSA Decryption Proof
nodes.description: The proof that RSA decryption inverts encryption, relying on Euler's theorem and the relationship between the public and private exponents.

nodes.name: Digital Signatures
nodes.description: Cryptographic signatures authenticating a message by signing with a private key so that anyone can verify authenticity with the public key.

nodes.name: Polynomial Roots and Degree
nodes.description: Properties of polynomials over a field, including that a nonzero degree-d polynomial has at most d roots, used throughout the course.

nodes.name: Polynomial Interpolation
nodes.description: The fact that d+1 points uniquely determine a degree-d polynomial, recovered by Lagrange interpolation over a field.

nodes.name: Secret Sharing
nodes.description: Shamir's secret sharing splitting a secret among parties as points on a polynomial so that any sufficient subset can reconstruct it.

nodes.name: Error Correcting Codes
nodes.description: Polynomial-based codes such as Reed-Solomon adding redundancy so messages can be recovered despite a bounded number of errors or erasures.

nodes.name: Bijections and Cardinality
nodes.description: Comparing the sizes of sets using bijections, defining two sets as equinumerous when a one-to-one correspondence exists between them.

nodes.name: Cantor's Diagonalization
nodes.description: Cantor's diagonal argument constructing an element differing from every member of a list, proving that certain sets are uncountable.

nodes.name: Uncountability of Reals
nodes.description: The proof, via diagonalization, that the real numbers cannot be put in bijection with the naturals and are therefore uncountable.

nodes.name: The Halting Problem
nodes.description: The halting problem, the undecidable task of determining whether an arbitrary program halts on a given input, proved by diagonalization.

nodes.name: Undecidability
nodes.description: The existence of well-defined problems that no algorithm can solve for all inputs, established by reduction from the halting problem.

nodes.name: Basic Counting Rules
nodes.description: The fundamental sum and product rules counting the outcomes of disjoint choices and of sequences of independent choices.

nodes.name: Combinations and Permutations
nodes.description: Counting ordered selections (permutations) and unordered selections (combinations) of items from a set, with their factorial formulas.

nodes.name: Combinatorial Proofs
nodes.description: Proving identities by counting the same quantity in two different ways, showing that the two expressions must be equal.

nodes.name: Stars and Bars
nodes.description: The stars-and-bars technique counting the nonnegative integer solutions of an equation, equivalently distributions of identical items into bins.

nodes.name: Inclusion-Exclusion
nodes.description: The inclusion-exclusion principle counting the size of a union by alternately adding and subtracting the sizes of intersections.

nodes.name: Probability Spaces
nodes.description: A probability space comprising a sample space of outcomes, events as subsets, and a probability measure satisfying Kolmogorov's axioms.

nodes.name: Conditional Probability
nodes.description: The probability of an event given that another has occurred, defined by normalising their joint probability by the conditioning event's probability.

nodes.name: Bayes' Rule
nodes.description: Bayes' rule inverting conditional probabilities to update the probability of a hypothesis given evidence, combining priors and likelihoods.

nodes.name: Event Independence
nodes.description: Two events are independent when the occurrence of one does not change the probability of the other, equivalently their joint equals the product.

nodes.name: Discrete Random Variables
nodes.description: Random variables taking values in a discrete set, described by a probability mass function assigning probabilities to each possible value.

nodes.name: Expectation
nodes.description: The expectation of a random variable, its probability-weighted average value, summarising the centre of its distribution.

nodes.name: Linearity of Expectation
nodes.description: The property that the expectation of a sum equals the sum of expectations, holding even when the variables are dependent.

nodes.name: Variance and Covariance
nodes.description: Variance measuring a variable's spread about its mean, and covariance measuring the degree to which two variables vary together.

nodes.name: Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
nodes.description: The Bernoulli distribution modelling a single success/failure trial and the binomial modelling the number of successes in independent trials.

nodes.name: Geometric Distribution
nodes.description: The geometric distribution modelling the number of independent Bernoulli trials until the first success, with its memoryless property.

nodes.name: Poisson Distribution
nodes.description: The Poisson distribution modelling counts of rare independent events in a fixed interval, the limit of the binomial for many trials.

nodes.name: Hypergeometric Distribution
nodes.description: The hypergeometric distribution modelling the number of successes when sampling without replacement from a finite population.

nodes.name: Continuous Random Variables
nodes.description: Random variables taking values over a continuum, described by a probability density rather than a probability mass function.

nodes.name: Probability Density Function
nodes.description: A probability density function whose integral over an interval gives the probability that the continuous variable falls within that interval.

nodes.name: Cumulative Distribution Function
nodes.description: The cumulative distribution function giving the probability that a random variable is at most a given value, defined for any distribution.

nodes.name: Uniform and Exponential Distributions
nodes.description: The uniform distribution spreading probability evenly over an interval and the memoryless exponential distribution modelling waiting times.

nodes.name: Normal Distribution
nodes.description: The normal (Gaussian) distribution, a symmetric bell-shaped law parametrised by mean and variance, central to statistics and the central limit theorem.

nodes.name: Markov's Inequality
nodes.description: Markov's inequality bounding the probability that a nonnegative random variable exceeds a value using only its mean.

nodes.name: Chebyshev's Inequality
nodes.description: Chebyshev's inequality bounding the probability that a variable deviates far from its mean using its variance.

nodes.name: Chernoff Bounds
nodes.description: Chernoff bounds giving exponentially decaying tail bounds for sums of independent random variables via the moment-generating function.

nodes.name: Weak Law of Large Numbers
nodes.description: The weak law of large numbers stating the sample mean of independent identically distributed variables converges in probability to the true mean.

nodes.name: Central Limit Theorem
nodes.description: The central limit theorem stating that the normalised sum of many independent variables converges in distribution to a normal distribution.

nodes.name: Markov Chains Basics
nodes.description: Markov chains modelling random processes that transition between states with probabilities depending only on the current state.

nodes.name: Hitting Times
nodes.description: Hitting times, the expected number of steps for a Markov chain to first reach a specified state from a given starting state.

nodes.name: Stationary Distributions
nodes.description: A stationary distribution unchanged by the chain's transitions, describing the long-run fraction of time spent in each state.

nodes.name: PageRank Algorithm
nodes.description: PageRank ranking web pages by the stationary distribution of a random-surfer Markov chain over the hyperlink graph.
